headline: Utah launches AI-powered medical diagnosis and prescription without human oversight
summary: A new app scans faces, analyzes skin, and recommends medication for acne, marking a first for AI in direct patient care.
details: Utah is pioneering a new era in healthcare by becoming the first state to allow an AI to examine patients and prescribe medication without direct human oversight. A healthcare startup, Nolla Health, has launched a limited, one-year program focused on treating mild-to-moderate acne.

The Nolla Health app requires users to scan their face, fill out a medical history, and then an AI analyzes the skin to determine an acne severity score. Based on this score and the user's medical information, the AI recommends one of eight approved topical medications.

Initially, the first 100 prescriptions will undergo review by human doctors before being sent to pharmacies. The subsequent 400 patients will have their AI-generated prescriptions reviewed retrospectively by a physician weekly, with a final phase involving monthly reviews of at least 10% of prescriptions.

This development raises significant questions about the role of AI in medicine, especially after past incidents where AI-driven health advice led to adverse outcomes, such as a man developing bromism from following ChatGPT's dietary recommendations. Google also recently removed AI features from its search due to inaccurate health information.

Nolla Health CEO Luis Wenus stated that the approved medications have limited side effects, primarily localized skin irritation or dryness, and are topical only. This controlled approach aims to mitigate risks associated with AI-prescribed treatments.

While this program is small in scope, it represents a potential first step towards AI playing a more significant role in treating less severe medical conditions, challenging the long-held assumption that healthcare is largely immune to AI-driven job displacement.
